```{r setup}
library(bwebs)
```

This vignette goes through the whole workflow of *bwebs* (Amador Crespo
and Rico 2026b) on the invented example
community of the package and explains the methodological decisions behind
each step: how links are inferred, how their probabilities are calibrated,
how the default matching rule was chosen and how it performs on an
independent food web.

## 1. The community and its nodes

A community is described by two tables. The **nodes** have one row per taxon
(or non-taxonomic resource, such as detritus), with its classification
aligned with the names of the registry, its role and its rank of
identification:

```{r}
example_taxa[, c("node_id", "taxon", "rank", "role", "family", "order", "class")]
```

The **community** has one row per sample and node, in long format, with an
abundance or biomass. Only presence is used: a node is present when its value
is greater than `threshold` (0 by default). A zero is an observed absence;
`NA` is unknown and is never treated as an absence.

```{r}
head(example_community)
```

`prepare_nodes()` validates the nodes and computes, for each node and role,
the levels at which it is matched with the registry. Detritus is matched by
name and alias; producers and detritus never consume; the shrimp
*Dugastella valentina*, absent from the registry, takes the records of
*Asellus* through an explicit surrogate.

```{r}
nodes <- prepare_nodes(example_taxa)
nodes
```

## 2. The metaweb and the evidence of each link

`build_metaweb()` infers the potential links with the WebBuilder logic of
Gray et al. (2015): a link resource → consumer exists if a record of the
registry matches both nodes at their levels. The default `matching_rule()`
starts at family level and climbs to order and class until a node links with
at least five other nodes of the community, using every registry at every
level (section 4 shows how this rule was chosen). The package includes two
registries that can be distributed, that of Gray et al. (2015) (`gray2015`)
and the freshwater food webs of GATEWAy (Brose et al. 2019; `gateway`), and
the examples combine them:

```{r}
reg <- combine_registries(gray2015, gateway)
mw <- build_metaweb(nodes, reg)
mw
head(mw$edges[, c("resource", "consumer", "support", "n_sources", "evidence_class")])
```

Each link keeps the **class of evidence** of its best supporting record: the
taxonomic generalisation needed to reach it (`exact` when the record names
the node itself, then `genus`, `subfamily`, `family`, `order`, `class`, or
`generic` for generic resources such as "Algae"). It also keeps how much
evidence supports it: the records and studies (`n_records`, `n_sources`),
the consumer and resource taxa among them (`n_consumer_taxa`: the consumer
and its relatives that eat the resource or its relatives;
`n_resource_taxa`: those relatives of the resource) and the relatives of
each node with records in the network (`n_consumer_known`,
`n_resource_known`):

```{r}
head(mw$edges[, c("resource", "consumer", "evidence_class", "n_sources",
                  "n_consumer_taxa", "n_consumer_known")])
```

## 3. Calibration: how often are inferred links observed?

A metaweb built from a compilation contains links that are not realised in a
given community, and more so the more taxonomic generalisation they needed.
`validate_rule()` measures this on the registry itself: each validation
study (a whole community with recorded diets) is left out in turn, rebuilt
from the rest of the registry with the same rule, and the inferred links are
compared with those recorded in it.

Studies of the same system share records. If one of them stays in the
registry while the other is rebuilt, its records predict the other and the
probabilities are overestimated. `shared_studies()` finds them:

```{r}
validation_webs <- gray2015_sources$study_id[gray2015_sources$validation]
shared_studies(gray2015, validation_webs, threshold = 0.2)
```

62% of the links of study 13 are also recorded in study 50, so the two are
left out together (`groups`). Study 12 is Tuesday Lake (section 5).

`calibrate_links()` then fits a logistic model with one coefficient per
class of evidence and a random effect of the web to the counts of inferred
and observed links. It is a Bayesian model: the coefficients have normal
priors (standard deviation `prior_sd = 1.5` on the logit scale) and the
standard deviation of the web effect a half-normal prior (scale
`prior_sigma = 2.5`); the web effects are integrated out by adaptive
Gauss-Hermite quadrature and the posterior is sampled by Metropolis-Hastings
(`diagnostics$rhat` should be close to 1 and `diagnostics$ess` large). The
package includes the calibrations of the Gray et al. (2015) registry alone
(`gray2015_calibration`), combined with GloBI (`gray2015_globi_calibration`)
and combined with GATEWAy, the one of the examples:

```{r}
gray2015_gateway_calibration
gray2015_gateway_calibration$webs[, c("study_id", "n_consumers", "n_predicted", "precision")]
```

`p_average` is the probability in a web with an average effect and `p_new`
the probability in a new system, averaged over web effects. Two results
matter for the interpretation:

* Links supported by records of the taxon itself or of its genus are
  observed more often than links that needed a family, and these more often
  than links that needed an order or a class: the class of evidence is
  informative. The classes are ordered (`monotone = TRUE`, the default), so
  that a link supported by a closer relative is never less probable than
  one supported by a more distant relative; neighbouring classes that the
  validation webs do not separate share their probability. With a free
  coefficient per class (`calibrate_links(monotone = FALSE)`) links of the
  same genus came out more probable than links of the same taxon, and links
  that needed a class more probable than links that needed an order; in the
  cross-validation of section 4 both versions predicted the webs left out
  equally well.
* The probability depends on the class only, not on the amount of evidence:
  in the same cross-validation, links supported by more studies, records or
  relatives (or by a larger share of the relatives of the consumer or of
  the resource) were not more often observed in the webs left out than the
  class predicts. Their effects changed sign from one registry to another,
  since they reflect how much each group has been studied rather than how
  probable the link is.
* The proportion of inferred links that are observed varies a lot between
  webs (the standard deviation of the web effect on the logit scale is
  `r round(gray2015_gateway_calibration$sigma, 2)`): part of it reflects differences
  between systems, part how completely each web was described.

The probability of a link is the probability of observing it in a comparable,
well-studied community. Because validation webs miss rare links, it is a
lower bound for the existence of the link.

### Pairs without an inferred link: the taxonomic decay

The rule infers a link only where the registry has records close enough to
both nodes. The other pairs are not impossible: in the validation webs,
`r round(100 * sum(gray2015_gateway_calibration$decay$counts$observed) / sum(gray2015_gateway_calibration$decay$counts$pairs))`%
of the pairs without an inferred link are recorded links. With
`matching_rule(decay = TRUE)` (the default), `validate_rule()` also records
how close the registry comes to each of those pairs: the closest level at
which relatives of the consumer have recorded diets (its family, order,
class, phylum or any consumer) and the closest level at which the resource
is related to a resource of those diets (within the family of a recorded
resource, order, class, phylum or not related), and whether a record of a
generic group applies to it. `calibrate_links()` fits a second model of the
same form to these counts, with its own web effect, with effects that never
increase with the distance and with an effect of the size of the web (per
unit of log(nodes / 50)), since connectance usually falls as webs grow:

```{r}
gray2015_gateway_calibration$decay$effects[, c("side", "level", "estimate", "std_error")]
```

The consumer effects are on the logit scale for a resource not related to
the recorded diet, in a web of 50 nodes; the resource effects are added to
them. `sample_metawebs()` uses the number of nodes of the metaweb, and
`score_metaweb()` the number of nodes evaluated. With Gray + GATEWAy a
resource within the family of a recorded resource raises the probability,
and consumers whose closest relatives with records are in another phylum
get much less; with the Gray registry alone the decay mostly gives these
pairs the rate at which the rule misses links, and the relation of the
resource to the recorded diet barely changes it. With GloBI the rule misses
fewer links and the decay is lower (section 10). In the validation webs every taxon eats or is
eaten, so these probabilities may be too high for communities sampled
independently of their diets; Tuesday Lake (section 5) is a check.
`matching_rule(decay = FALSE)` gives these pairs probability 0, as in
WebBuilder.

Which studies count as whole communities is a scientific decision. The
bundled calibration uses a provisional set (`gray2015_sources$validation`);
to use another one, validate and calibrate again (a few minutes):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
my_sources <- c("27", "13", "50", "12", "59", "63", "11", "15", "58", "46", "49")
v <- validate_rule(gray2015, sources = my_sources, groups = list(c("13", "50")))
my_calibration <- calibrate_links(v, seed = 1)
```

## 4. Choosing the matching rule and the sources

How far should a node climb, and from where? `score_rule()` answers with a
cross-validated **Brier score**: each validation system is left out of the
calibration in turn, its inferred links take the probability of their class
in a new system under the calibration fitted to the other systems, pairs
without an inferred link take probability 0, and the squared errors against
the recorded links are averaged over all the pairs of the web (lower is
better). A missed link costs 1, an inferred link of probability \(p\) costs
\((1 - p)^2\) when it is real and \(p^2\) when it is not, so the score
rewards both finding the links and giving them the right probabilities. The
`skill` compares it with a null model that gives every pair the mean
connectance of the other systems, and `tss` is the true skill statistic of
the deterministic metaweb, as in Gray et al. (2015). With the taxonomic
decay, the pairs without an inferred link take instead the probability of
their evidence under the decay model fitted to the other systems. The rules
and the sources below were compared without the decay (it was added
afterwards, in version 0.3.0).

`compare_rules()` scores a list of rules on the same webs; `candidate_rules()`
is the grid of 21 rules (fixed matching at the taxon, genus, family or
order; climbing from genus or family to order or class with thresholds of 1
or 5 partners; the WebBuilder ladder up to family, order or class; three
rules without downward inheritance). With the Gray registry alone (Tuesday
Lake kept apart, section 5), the comparison takes about half an hour, so its
result is included:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
registry <- gray2015[gray2015$study_id != "12", ]   # Tuesday Lake kept apart
sources <- setdiff(validation_webs, "12")
cmp <- compare_rules(registry, sources = sources, groups = list(c("13", "50")), seed = 2026)
```

```{r}
gray2015_rule_comparison[, c("rule", "brier", "brier_diff", "brier_diff_se", "skill", "tss",
                             "precision", "recall")]
```

Climbing from family to class had the lowest score. The threshold (one or
five partners) and the downward inheritance made no difference larger than
its standard error; starting at genus, using the ladder of Gray et al.
(2015) or matching at a fixed level scored worse, and matching only the
taxon itself scored worst. With the Gray registry alone the skill of every
rule is slightly negative: a third of the recorded links are not inferred.

The eight main rules were then scored with records of Global Biotic
Interactions (GloBI, section 10) for the consumers of the validation webs,
alone and combined with the Gray registry. When each web was rebuilt, the
GloBI studies holding at least 10% of its links (copies of that web in
other compilations) were left out too (`validate_rule(exclusions = )`):

```{r}
source_comparison[1:12, c("source", "primary_registry", "supplementary_max_level", "rule",
                          "brier", "diff_vs_gray", "diff_vs_gray_se", "skill", "recall")]
```

Both registries used at every level (no primary registry) with the default
rule scored best, and this combination sets the defaults of
`matching_rule()`. GloBI raised the share of recorded links that are inferred
from two thirds to nine tenths without lowering the precision (about 40%),
and the skill became positive. Using GloBI only up to family
(`primary_registry = "gray2015"`, `supplementary_max_level = "family"`)
scored worse than using it at every level. GloBI holds secondary
compilations (metawebs and trait databases) that may contain the
validation webs generalised to family or order, which the exclusions by
shared links do not detect; without them the scores were nearly the same
(`dev/validation/source_sensitivity.R` in the GitHub repository of the
package). The rule itself was again best climbing from family, with any
source.

The freshwater food webs of GATEWAy (Brose et al. 2019; `gateway`, with the
webs that copy a validation web left out with it) were compared later,
with the default rule and the decay: they lowered the Brier score of the
Gray registry from 0.209 to 0.205, but raised that of Gray + GloBI from
0.197 to 0.201. Gray + GloBI is therefore the best combination, and Gray +
GATEWAy the best one that the package can include
(`gray2015_gateway_calibration`; GloBI records cannot be redistributed).

## 5. An independent test: Tuesday Lake

The Tuesday Lake food webs of 1984 and 1986 (Cohen et al. 2003; Jonsson et
al. 2005), from the *cheddar* package (Hudson et al. 2013), are an independent
test: study 12 of the registry is Tuesday Lake, so it was left out of the
registry and of the validation webs while the rules and the sources were
compared, and so were the GloBI studies that copy it.

```{r}
head(tuesday_lake_taxa[, c("node_id", "taxon", "rank", "role", "family", "class")])
table(tuesday_lake_links$sample_id)
```

`score_metaweb()` compares a metaweb with an observed web. For the test, the
metaweb is built from the registry without study 12 and the calibration is
fitted to the other 12 webs:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
v <- validate_rule(registry, sources = sources, groups = list(c("13", "50")))
cal <- calibrate_links(v, seed = 2026)
mw_tl <- build_metaweb(prepare_nodes(tuesday_lake_taxa), registry)
tl84 <- tuesday_lake_links[tuesday_lake_links$sample_id == "TL84", ]
present <- tuesday_lake_community$node_id[tuesday_lake_community$sample_id == "TL84"]
score_metaweb(mw_tl, cal, tl84, nodes = present)
```

The scores on Tuesday Lake (mean of the two years) are in the same tables:

```{r}
source_comparison[1:12, c("source", "rule", "tl_brier", "tl_skill", "tl_tss", "tl_precision",
                          "tl_recall")]
```

The default inferred about 70% of the observed links (a fifth with the Gray
registry alone, mostly British streams with few diets of plankton) and had
a positive skill; the ranking of the combinations on Tuesday Lake agreed
with the cross-validation (Spearman correlation 0.73). Links inferred from
generic resources ("Algae" extended to every alga) are frequent in the
validation streams but rare in this plankton web, so their calibrated
probability is too high there.

The scores above are those of the rule alone. With the taxonomic decay
(section 3), the pairs without an inferred link take the probability of
their evidence, and on Tuesday Lake every score improved: with Gray + GloBI
the Brier score went from 0.147 to 0.141 (1984) and from 0.160 to 0.154
(1986), and the decay expected a few links fewer among the pairs not
inferred than the rule had missed (68 and 55, against 78 and 69 observed).
Among taxa, the webs sampled with the decay came close to the observed ones
in connectance, mean trophic level and proportion of top taxa, which the
rule alone underestimated. The decay does not know body size, though: it
also gives some probability to pairs that size would exclude, and most
consumers of the sampled webs were omnivores (0.84 of the trophic species
in 1984, against 0.50 observed). With the body masses of each year (section
6), the Brier score went down to 0.138 and 0.151 and the omnivores to 0.69,
while the top taxa rose to 0.07 (0.02 observed). With Gray + GATEWAy, the
registries of the examples, the scores with the masses were 0.139 and 0.137,
the best of the three combinations in 1986. These scores are those of free
coefficients of the classes of evidence; with the ordered classes of the
default (section 3), the scores with the masses went down to 0.132 and
0.139 with Gray + GloBI and to 0.136 and 0.133 with Gray + GATEWAy, and up
to 0.146 and 0.147 with the Gray registry alone (`dev/validation/results.md`
in the GitHub repository of the package).

## 6. Plausible metawebs

`sample_metawebs()` takes the coefficients and the standard deviation of the
web effect of each draw from the posterior draws of the calibration and,
with `system = "random"`, draws the effect of the system, and keeps each link
with the probability of its class. One realisation of the metaweb is shared
by all the samples of the community in each draw.

```{r}
draws <- sample_metawebs(mw, gray2015_gateway_calibration, n_draws = 100, seed = 2026)
draws
head(draws$links[, c("resource", "consumer", "evidence_class", "p_mean", "inclusion")])
```

With `system = "average"` the system effect is fixed at 0 (a community like
the average validation web) and the intervals are narrower; a number fixes it
at that value on the logit scale.

With the taxonomic decay, every pair without a link of the metaweb
(`mw$decay`) is drawn too, with the probability of its evidence and an
effect of the system of its own, drawn independently of that of the classes.
These links are kept apart, as the rows of `draws$background$pairs` present
in each draw, and `calc_indicators()` adds them to the web of every sample:

```{r}
head(draws$background$pairs[, c("resource", "consumer", "consumer_level", "resource_level",
                                 "p_mean")])
```

### The matrix of link probabilities

`link_probabilities()` gives the probability of every resource → consumer
pair, the matrix from which the draws come: each inferred link with the
probability of its class in a new system (`p_new`), each pair without a link
with that of its evidence for the decay, manual links 1 and cannibalism 0.
A pair of probability 0.25 is present in about one draw in four:

```{r}
P <- link_probabilities(mw, gray2015_gateway_calibration)
round(P[c("cocconeis_placentula", "cpom", "baetis_rhodani", "simulium"),
        c("gammarus_pulex", "cordulegaster_boltonii")], 2)
inc <- draws$links$inclusion
p_links <- P[cbind(draws$links$resource, draws$links$consumer)]
summary(inc - p_links)
```

In a draw the links share the parameters and the effect of the system, so
the number of links varies more among draws than among webs drawn link by
link from `P`; the probability of each pair is the same. With
`system = "average"` or a number, `link_probabilities()` fixes the effect
of the system as `sample_metawebs()` does, and with `masses` it includes
the size term.

### Body masses

The links of a predator also depend on the size of its prey, which the
registry does not know. With `masses`, `sample_metawebs()` shifts the
probability of every predation pair (an animal resource) by the effect of
the predator/prey mass ratio of `size_model`: 0 at the optimum ratio and
lower the further the ratio is from it, fitted to the aquatic webs of
GATEWAy, with weights for the links inferred by the rule and for the pairs
of the taxonomic decay chosen by the validation by folds (the 12 validation
webs with body masses, left out by system):

```{r}
size_model
```

The masses can be one per node, as here for Tuesday Lake (the unit does not
matter, only the ratios), or a matrix with one row per node and one column
per draw. With the masses of the draws of a biomass model (such as
`simulate()` of *bmassa*; Amador Crespo and Rico 2026a), each realization
of the web uses the masses of its
own draw, so that the links of a realization and the masses and biomasses of
its taxa come from the same draw:

```{r}
masses <- tapply(tuesday_lake_community$mass_kg, tuesday_lake_community$node_id, mean)
reg_tl <- combine_registries(gray2015[gray2015$study_id != "12", ], gateway)
mw_tl <- build_metaweb(prepare_nodes(tuesday_lake_taxa), reg_tl)
draws_tl <- sample_metawebs(mw_tl, gray2015_gateway_calibration, n_draws = 200,
                            masses = masses, seed = 1)
draws_tl
```

Draws with and without `masses` use the same random numbers, so a draw
loses only the links that the size term makes improbable.

With a matrix of masses, draw `d` of the result is one realization of the
web: its links (column `d` of `z` and element `d` of `background$present`)
and the masses of its nodes (column `d` of `masses`). Here the masses of
each draw are invented, with a log-normal error of 20%; in an analysis they
would come from the draws of a biomass model, so that the biomasses of the
same draw go with that web:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
m_draws <- matrix(masses, length(masses), 200, dimnames = list(names(masses), NULL)) *
  exp(matrix(stats::rnorm(length(masses) * 200, 0, 0.2), length(masses)))
draws_m <- sample_metawebs(mw_tl, gray2015_gateway_calibration, n_draws = 200,
                           masses = m_draws, seed = 1)
d <- 1
web_1 <- rbind(draws_m$links[draws_m$z[, d], c("resource", "consumer")],
               draws_m$background$pairs[draws_m$background$present[[d]],
                                        c("resource", "consumer")])
nrow(web_1)
head(draws_m$masses[, d])
```

## 7. Indicators of every sample

`calc_indicators()` builds the web of each sample in each draw (the nodes
present plus the permanent resources) and computes the indicators of
`web_indicators()` on the web without cannibalism and without isolated nodes,
aggregated into trophic species. Modularity (with *igraph*; Csardi and Nepusz 2006) and robustness are
optional because they are slower.

```{r}
ind <- calc_indicators(draws, example_community, permanent = c("cpom", "fpom"))
head(ind$values[, c("draw", "sample_id", "S", "L", "C", "TL_mean", "prop_omnivores")])
table(ind$values$status)
```

In draws with a very negative system effect the metaweb keeps few links, and
a sample can be left without any: its indicators are then undefined
(`status = "empty_web"`), not zero. By default the summaries report such
draws as missing; with `na_rm = TRUE` they are left out and counted in
`n_missing`, and the summaries then describe the draws where the indicator is
defined.

## 8. Summaries and contrasts

`summarize_indicators()` summarises the draws by sample or by groups of
samples; `contrast_indicators()` compares groups within each draw, which
keeps the uncertainty shared by all the samples of a draw out of the
contrast.

```{r}
summarize_indicators(ind, indicators = c("S", "C", "TL_mean"), samples = example_samples,
                     by = "treatment", na_rm = TRUE)[, c(1:7, 13)]
contrast_indicators(ind, example_samples, by = "treatment", reference = "control",
                    indicators = c("S", "C", "TL_mean"), na_rm = TRUE)[, c(1, 3:8, 10)]
```

The deterministic metaweb gives the reference values of the potential webs:

```{r}
det <- calc_indicators(mw, example_community, permanent = c("cpom", "fpom"))
summarize_indicators(det, indicators = c("S", "C", "TL_mean"),
                     samples = example_samples, by = "treatment")[, 1:4]
```

## 9. Energy fluxes

`calc_fluxes()` computes the energy fluxes of every sample in every
realization with the food-web energetics approach of the *fluxweb* package
(Gauzens et al. 2019): at steady state, the energy a consumer assimilates
from its resources equals its metabolic losses plus what its consumers take
from it. The losses come from the body mass of each population and the
temperature (Brown et al. 2004), and the efficiencies from the type of
resource (Polazzo et al. 2023); any of them can be replaced:

```{r}
flux_parameters()
```

Brown et al. (2004) estimated an activation energy of 0.69 eV across all
groups, the value of Polazzo et al. (2023), but fitted the intercepts to
rates corrected for temperature with 0.63 eV, the value used by default.
`flux_parameters("polazzo_2023")` uses 0.69 eV, with which the losses, and
so all the fluxes, are about 11 times lower at 20 °C.

The populations give the biomass of every node of each sample (g of wet
mass per unit of the sampling basis, here per sample) and the mean
individual mass of the consumers (g of wet mass); a node can have several
populations, such as the life stages of a taxon, whose losses are added.
`node_masses()` gives the masses of the nodes for the size term, so that
realization `d` has the links drawn with the masses of draw `d` and the
biomasses of the same draw:

```{r}
masses <- node_masses(mw, example_populations)
draws_f <- sample_metawebs(mw, gray2015_gateway_calibration, n_draws = 100, masses = masses,
                           seed = 2026)
fl <- calc_fluxes(draws_f, example_populations, temperature = 15, engine = "internal")
fl
contrast_indicators(fl, example_samples, by = "treatment", reference = "control",
                    indicators = c("total_flux", "herbivory", "detritivory", "carnivory"),
                    na_rm = TRUE)[, c(3:8, 10)]
```

`engine = "fluxweb"`, the default, solves the same equations with
`fluxweb::fluxing()`; `engine = "internal"` gives the same fluxes without
*fluxweb*. The fluxes are in W (J/s) per unit of the sampling basis.

A consumer that no path of links reaches from a producer or detritus in a
realization is left out of its fluxes (`n_unsupported`). A realization whose
consumers take most of their diet from one another, which happens in draws
with few inferred links, where the links of the taxonomic decay among
consumers make up most diets, has no steady state (`status = "unsolved"`):
assimilation loses energy at every step, so such loops cannot sustain
themselves. These realizations are energetically implausible, and
`na_rm = TRUE` leaves them out of the summaries:

```{r}
table(fl$values$status)
```

With *bmassa*, the draws of `simulate()` hold the mass of every
population of the abundance table in each draw, with the errors shared as
in its totals; `calc_fluxes()` takes them directly, together with a table of
the biomasses of producers and detritus, and the abundances of all the
groups must share the sampling basis:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
est <- bmassa::estimate_biomass(abundance, taxa, lengths)  # with sample_id and node_id
sim <- simulate(bmassa::convert_currency(est, to = "wet_mass", unit = "mg"), nsim = 1000,
                seed = 1)
draws <- sample_metawebs(mw, gray2015_gateway_calibration, n_draws = 1000,
                         masses = node_masses(mw, sim), seed = 1)
fl <- calc_fluxes(draws, list(sim, basal_biomass), temperature = temperature_by_sample)
```

## 10. GloBI and other registries

`fetch_globi()` downloads trophic interactions from Global Biotic
Interactions and `globi_to_registry()` converts them (an internet connection
is needed, so this is not run here). Query each consumer of the community by
name, genus and family, as for `gray2015_globi_calibration`. GloBI already
contains the Gray et al. (2015) and Brose et al. (2005) compilations, which
are dropped by default, and other copies of classic food webs: check them
with `shared_studies()`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
taxa <- unique(c(example_taxa$taxon, example_taxa$genus, example_taxa$family))
raw <- fetch_globi(taxa[!is.na(taxa)], cache_dir = "globi_cache")
globi <- globi_to_registry(raw)
both <- combine_registries(gray2015, globi)
mw2 <- build_metaweb(nodes, both)
draws2 <- sample_metawebs(mw2, gray2015_globi_calibration, n_draws = 100, seed = 2026)
```

`gray2015_globi_calibration` is the calibration of the default rule with the
Gray registry combined with GloBI (13 validation webs, with the GloBI copies
of each web left out when it was rebuilt), the best combination of the
cross-validation (section 4):

```{r}
gray2015_globi_calibration
```

A metaweb and its calibration must use the same rule and the same
registries: `sample_metawebs()` warns when the registries differ, because
the probability of each class of evidence depends on them, and links
supported only by registries outside the calibration have no probability
(`uncalibrated = `). To calibrate another combination, validate it with the
GloBI records of the consumers of the validation webs
(`validate_rule(train_registries = , exclusions = )`; see
`dev/globi/` and `dev/validation/` in the GitHub repository of the
package).
